CHAPTER WRITTEN CONTENT

Predator–Prey Population Dynamics with Infradian Rhythms

What are Predators, Prey, and Infradian Rhythms?

  • Learning Objective: Define predators, prey, and infradian rhythms, and explain the interconnected relationship between them.

In an ecological setting, predators and prey have an interconnected relationship: one hunts the other for survival, while the other hides. As the Earth developed from the earliest stage, the Last Universal Common Ancestor, also known as LUCA, evolved into different organisms. As ancestral animals got exposed to different environmental factors and genetic mutations, they underwent evolutionary changes that caused them to develop different features, appearances, and adaptations over time. Predators, animals that naturally hunt other animals for food, often possess certain traits that assist them in the predation process. For instance, snakes and scorpions produce neurotoxic venoms to subdue prey, cheetahs have specialized body structures that allow them to hunt prey faster, and crocodiles have great ambush tactics. On the other hand, prey, animals that are caught and killed by predators for food, have also developed adaptations that allow them to maintain survival. For example, skunks have foul-smelling chemicals in their internal body systems, turtles have shells to prevent physical damage from predators, and nocturnal animals are specialized in avoidance strategies to hide away from others.

Infradian rhythms are connected to the predator–prey cycle in many different aspects. First, the evolutionary changes and genetic mutations that both species undergo are classified as infradian rhythms, as these are continual cycles that last longer than a 24-hour period. In addition, seasonal variation in certain ecosystems causes behavioral or physiological changes in both predators and prey. This aspect contributes to the fluctuation in predator–prey populations. Generally, since the populations of predators and prey change dynamically in a cycle, this allows scientists to collect sample data and discover patterns and trends in species’ responses to changes. Many of the behaviors exhibited by different animal species can be classified into the same category according to rationales proposed by ecologists. For example, bears, rats, and turtles all experience the hibernation process in the winter to conserve internal energy, also taking into account that there is a scarcity of food and resources during that season. This behavioral pattern allows scientists to recognize how common hibernation is among different animal species, leading them to classify it as an infradian rhythm instance. From an ecological perspective, infradian rhythms are not only cycles that last more than 24 hours, but they are also one of the vital processes that maintain long-term stability in the ecosystem.

The Predator and Prey Population Cycle in the Ecosystem

  • Learning Objective: Demonstrate the predator and prey population cycle in the ecosystem and question the changes in their population over time.

Predator–prey dynamics are natural occurrences when the population sizes of predators and prey in a community are not constant over time, and they sometimes fluctuate in opposite directions (Ha, 2022). In the ecosystem, this pattern can be seen between many types of predators and prey. One salient example is the change in population size of snowshoe hares and lynxes. Snowshoe hares, scientifically known as Lepus americanus, are herbivorous mammals that reside in the boreal forests of North America (National Park Service, 2021). In terms of infradian rhythms, snowshoe hare populations cycle in eight- to eleven-year periods, meaning that the population returns to its original level in eight to eleven years of time. Additionally, the species has evolved some adaptations in its living environment that allow it to have survival advantages over others. For instance, snowshoe hares have extremely fast agility: they can run up to 27 miles per hour, allowing them to escape from slow-moving predators (Kline, 2024). Moreover, snowshoe hares are prey for various predators due to their rapid reproductive rate: they breed at about one year of age and have two to three litters per year (Alaska Department of Fish and Game, n.d.), with one to nine young per litter. Hence, the prevalence of the Lepus americanus in the ecosystem makes it prone to being targeted by many animals, one being lynxes. Since Canadian lynxes, scientifically named Lynx canadensis, are predators of the snowshoe hare, Canadian lynxes also predominantly dwell in northern North America (Fish & Wildlife Service, n.d.). They are mid-sized boreal forest carnivores and are also classified as mammals. Snowshoe hares are the primary food source of the lynx, suggesting that the population cycles of these two species are closely linked.

Figure 1 presents the predator–prey dynamics of the two studied species. The

population of snowshoe hares initially increases due to their high reproductive rates. This increase in prey population attracts more predators to the area and allows predators to have more food available for growth and reproduction, causing the population of lynxes to rise accordingly. When the population of predators increases, more prey would be physically consumed by predators, which lowers snowshoe hare population size. This decline in snowshoe hare population level contributes to a scarcity of food resources for lynx, thereby gradually diminishing the predator’s population size. This pattern repeats over and over again, which forms an infradian cycle in the ecosystem. Moreover, snowshoe hares and lynxes are not the only two species in which their population fluctuates repeatedly: most of the predator and prey populations resemble the population pattern which can be generalized into the predator–prey dynamics diagram shown in Figure 2.

Furthermore, it is important to note that this generalized population graph involves both top-down and bottom-up controls (Figure 3). When a population is mainly limited by predators, top-down control influences and exerts forces on the population size. In this case, when the population of predators rises, the predation pressure significantly limits the prey population, leading to a diminishing number of prey in the area. Conversely, bottom-up control is when the population is heavily dependent on the availability of resources or the bottom level of the food chain. For instance, when the prey population peaks, this indicates that predators have abundant food sources, which allows a significant increase in the population of predators. However, when the prey population reaches its trough, that signifies less food availability for predators, which in turn causes a considerable drop in predator population.

What Factors Drive or Maintain the Periodic Infradian Population Cycles in Predator–Prey

Systems?

Learning Objectives:

  • Differentiate and explain distinct types of factors that contribute to the periodic infradian population cycles in predator–prey systems.
  • Evaluate how abiotic variables affect the stability of populations in the predator–prey cycle.
  • Evaluate how resource and habitat factors contribute to population variation in the predator–prey cycle.
  • Evaluate how community factors affect the stability of populations in the predator–prey cycle.
  • Evaluate how biological and evolutionary variables influence the population change in the predator–prey cycle.

Although most predator–prey population dynamics resemble the generalized pattern shown in Figure 2, there are many instances where prey and predators resist changes in population through their evolved adaptations, environmental changes, and habitat structures. Both prey and predators evolve through natural selection, in which certain favorable traits allow species to survive longer compared to other less well-adapted organisms in the environment. Hence, it is important to consider the external factors that contribute to the maintenance of the periodic infradian population cycle in predator–prey systems, including but not limited to abiotic factors, resource and habitat factors, community factors, and biological and evolutionary variables.

  1. Abiotic Factors Abiotic factors contribute to population variation among predator and prey populations. Abiotic factors are the non-living components of the environment that influence the growth of organisms (BiologyOnline, 2023). These include the impact of sunlight, water, and temperature on the population size of species over time. One notable case study on how abiotic factors contribute to population change in prey is when Berg et al. investigated how rain serves as a density-independent factor for the population of aphids, a type of prey, in 2008. The study concluded that rain removed aphids from shoots and ears of wheat by 57% and 25%, respectively (Figure 4). These data later translated into the statistic that rain independently reduces aphid populations by 27%, serving as a significant mortality factor for aphid populations. Heavy rainfall also causes more aphids to be exposed to the ground, which is where their predators, ground-dwelling predatory arthropods, reside. This unexpected rise in prey exposure on the ground increases the arthropods’ consumption of aphids, which results in the prey population being considerably lower than the predator population in that specific time period. Hence, the decrease in prey population is not solely due to predation: extreme weather conditions are not negligible when evaluating population fluctuations among predators and prey.

Similarly, another research study also analyzed rainfall as a climate factor in predator–prey dynamics from various perspectives. It first outlines that when there is no rainfall, species experience drought in their environment. Low rainfall levels could potentially cause weaker body systems in prey, which makes them vulnerable to predators (Morin et al., 2021). Hence, this would increase predator population in the short run, but the predator population level would drop in the long run due to prey scarcity. From another point of view, high rainfall can contribute to vegetation growth, causing vegetation to become extremely dense in the area where predators and prey dwell. This rise in vegetation allows herbivorous prey to increase their growth rate and reproduce more frequently. Additionally, the dense vegetation can mutually help both the predators and prey in terms of survival and predation. For instance, dense vegetation assists predators like lions, leopards, and lynx to execute ambush attacks and tactics on prey, increasing predator population levels and diminishing prey population size. Conversely, densely formed vegetation can also help prey to conceal themselves from predators, which maintains the survival rate of prey. Hence, climate factors like rainfall do not universally benefit prey or predators in terms of population growth. It heavily depends on how predators and prey respond to the changes in abiotic factors.

  1. Resource and Habitat Factors Resource and habitat factors also have a significant impact on the population density of predators and prey. Resources in the ecosystem can include food, mates, and decomposers.

Specifically, food quantity serves as the main source of survival for snowshoe hares in the boreal forests of North America. As previously mentioned, snowshoe hares go through an approximate 10-year population cycle, in which nutrient abundance helps the prey increase its population density after a huge decline. Krebs et al. conducted an 8-year field experiment in a one km2 forest block in the Yukon to investigate how manipulating food supply, predator availability, and soil nutrient level would affect the population of snowshoe hare. While increasing fertilizer use in the control area helped the growth of plant biomass, it did not display a significant change in the population density of the targeted prey. Conversely, with a constant supply of supplemental food to the studied area, the population of snowshoe hare tripled during the cyclic peak and decline (Figure 5), revealing that food resource availability is the paramount factor that promotes population growth of the prey.

Furthermore, habitat structures of prey also play a pivotal role in the predator–prey dynamics. In 2025, Lennox et al. researched different ways in which prey’s habitats help them maintain survival in densely predator-populated environments. One notable instance from the research focuses on predator sculpin (Cottus gobio) and salmon (Salmo salar) eggs as the prey. In the ecosystem, habitat refers to the place in which a group of related organisms lives. Habitat is also commonly used as the area of refuge, and predation success for sculpin on salmon eggs is heavily dependent on how effectively the habitat can be used as refuge. Specifically, salmon eggs reside under substrates, which are layers of materials covering the bottom of a riverbed. When the substrates are smaller in size, it increases the protection layer density and reduces the accessible gap for predators to reach prey in the water, fully covering the salmon eggs for protection. Hence, the population level of salmon eggs is greatly affected by their habitat structure, making it a substantial factor to consider when evaluating population fluctuations of salmon eggs and sculpin.

  1. Community Factors The relationships of species in an ecosystem can be simplified into a complex, interconnected food web, where the diagram shows “what-eats-what” in an ecological community. Oftentimes, a predator does not have only one specific prey that they hunt for survival. Predators can also switch their target prey in order to maintain their dominant position in the ecosystem. For instance, tigers not only search for zebras as a food source, but they also have other prey to look for, including but not limited to wildebeests, buffaloes, and impalas. Interestingly, this mechanism, also known as predator switching, allows for the coexistence between different prey types (Archibald et al., 2023) by rendering sufficient time for the other prey species to grow in population size before the predator hunts for them. Hence, this ultimately stabilizes the food web model and predator–prey cycle by preventing the extinction of a certain species in the ecosystem.
  2. Biological and Evolutionary Factors Biological factors can be defined in many different ways. From an evolutionary aspect, biological factors that contribute to population variation can include animals evolving different traits that make them more adapted to the environment and less prone to being hunted by predators compared to other species. For example, chameleons can easily change the color of their skin to match the color of their background, confusing predators and allowing them to survive longer. From a different perspective, there are also other molecular biological processes that take place in the predator–prey cycle. One significant example is an observational experiment carried out by Sheriff et al. in 2009. Sheriff et al. found that when maternal snowshoe hares were under predation risk, their endocrine system gradually secreted a type of stress hormone called glucocorticoids. Simultaneously, it was also observed that the reproductive rate of snowshoe hares decreased constantly when they were under the pressure of being hunted by predators. Hence, the researchers concluded that higher stress levels, indicated by elevated glucocorticoid levels, were associated with lower reproduction in snowshoe hares, justifying the precipitous decline in prey population level when the predator population size surged.

Conclusion

In conclusion, the predator–prey cycle is a complicated yet continuous process that is prevalent in all ecosystems. The population sizes of both species fluctuate due to a range of reasons, ranging from environmental factors all the way to molecular biological factors. In order for the ecosystem to sustain and function properly, predators will keep hunting for prey, and prey will keep hiding away from the predators. This process will cause more evolutionary changes to occur in the ecosystem, and further research will be conducted to analyze the intricate system of predator–prey dynamics.
